Third, Herter and Situ (2021) called out “Building Energy Efficiency Standards Related to Load Management” (entered in Table A1 in the California State Energy Code). The Energy Code “consolidates demand response control requirements in California Code of Regulations, Title 24, Section 110.12, which includes the requirement for OpenADR certification or the ability to respond to a demand response signal from a certified OpenADR virtual end node, where applicable.” Other sections of the Energy Code that relate to or address load management include the following Joint Appendices (JA) to 2019 Title 24 Part 6 “Building Energy Efficiency Standards Rulemaking”: (1) JA-3 Time Dependent Valuation; (2) JA-5 Technical Specifications 74 for Occupant Controlled Smart Thermostats; (3) JA-11 Qualification Requirements for Photovoltaic System; (4) JA-12 Qualification Requirements for Battery System; and JA-13 Qualification Requirements for Heat Pump Water Heater Demand Management System. The second-to-last entry in Table A1 provides valuable context for some of the recent California policy concern about the need for increased load flexibility, as well as establishes two important dynamic pricing pilots which California continues to build on. This entry is the CPUC’s Rulemaking to Establish Policies, Processes, and Rules to Ensure Reliable Electric Service in California in the Event of an Extreme Weather Event in 2021 (R2011003). Amongst the many demand-side and supply-side provisions of the final Phase 2 Decision Directing the IOUS to Take Actions to Prepare for Potential Extreme Weather in the Summers of 2022 and 2023 (Decision 21-12-015 issued December 2, 2021) the CPUC adopted “two pilots that test how dynamic rates can cause customers to shift energy usage to off peak times, which can enhance system reliability in times of emergency. The first pilot, proposed by Valley Clean Energy (VCE), focuses on shifting agricultural water pumping to off peak times for reliability purposes through the use of dynamic rates and incentives. The second pilot, supported by SCE, uses TeMix’s technology to facilitate the use of dynamic rates as an incentive to shift load for customers using electric vehicles, behind the meter energy storage, and similar flexible technologies.” The final entry in Table A1 presents a major action by the CPUC, the Rulemaking to Advance Demand Flexibility through Electric Rates (R2207005). This CPUC Rulemaking encompasses several noteworthy individual and related actions. First, just before the Order Instituting Rulemaking was issued in July 2022, the CPUC Energy Division released a White Paper and Staff Proposal on June 22, 2022, “Advanced Strategies for Demand Flexibility Management and Customer DER Compensation.” The White Paper proposed a roadmap with a three-pillar structure of: Pillar 1, Price Presentation; Pillar 2, a 3-Prong Strategy for Rate Reform; and Pillar 3, Customer Options for Energy Optimization.
